items.title: Idolaters Break Jehovah's Heart
items.answer:
INTRODUCTION: When Jesus came up out of the baptismal water, heaven opened and Jehovah said: 'This is my Son, the beloved.' Our God is not a distant force or a set of laws. He has a heart — the Bible speaks of his eyes, his arms, his grief — and it can be moved, for good or for pain. That thought can make even a hard chapter like this week's reading, Ezekiel 5-6, precious, because it shows us a side of idolatry we rarely think about: not what idolatry does to the idolater, but what it does to our Creator. Let us walk through the three points in the study outline.

POINT 1 — Jehovah's people became steeped in idolatry. Ezekiel was already among the exiles in Babylon when Jehovah showed him what was going on back in Jerusalem. And the picture Jehovah painted was shocking: far from being better than the nations around her, Judah had become worse — 'She has rebelled against my judicial decisions and my statutes, acting more wickedly than the nations and the lands all around her.' (Eze 5:6, 7) The nations worshipped their gods out of ignorance; Judah worshipped idols in full knowledge of the truth, in Jehovah's own land, and finally inside his own sanctuary. Think of what that means: the very house that was to stand as a testimony to all the nations around — Jerusalem had been set 'in the middle of the nations' to represent Jehovah (Eze 5:5) — had become a museum of the idols of the surrounding peoples. To make the warning unforgettable, Jehovah gave Ezekiel strange instructions: shave your head and your beard — signs of humiliation and mourning — weigh the hair on scales, burn one third in the fire, strike another third with the sword all around the city, scatter the last third to the wind, and chase them with a drawn sword (Eze 5:1, 2, 12). Famine, war, and exile — that is what the hair on the prophet's head was preaching before he said a word. Idolatry was never a harmless private habit. It was treachery against a God who had done everything for his people.

POINT 2 — Their idolatry made Jehovah feel 'brokenhearted.' Now listen carefully to how Jehovah explains the coming judgment: '"'Therefore as surely as I am alive,' declares the Sovereign Lord Jehovah, 'because it was my sanctuary that you defiled with all your disgusting idols and with all your detestable practices, I will also reject you; my eye will not feel sorry, and I will show no compassion. (Eze 5:11) Notice the way he begins: 'as surely as I am alive.' Jehovah swears by his own life — by his very heart, we might say — before he describes what their worship had done to his sanctuary. This is not a court reading out a sentence. And to the remnant who would survive and be taken captive, Jehovah says something even more tender: 'And those who escape will remember me among the nations where they are taken captive. They will realize that I was brokenhearted over their unfaithful heart that turned away from me and at their eyes that are lusting after their disgusting idols. They will be ashamed of and loathe all the evil and detestable things they have done' (Eze 6:9) 'Brokenhearted' — that is the word. The Watchtower of May 15, 2004, page 6, paragraphs 2-3, drew out that thought: idolatry wounds Jehovah the way an unfaithful spouse wounds a loving mate, because his people had given their love to worthless things. The prophecies of Ezekiel, then, are not cold legal announcements. They carry the grief of a rejected Father. So the reading this week puts a question to every one of us: Am I giving Jehovah anything that competes with him for my heart? Anything I would fight to keep if he asked me to give it up? Notice too that Jehovah told the survivors that the escapees would remember him 'among the nations where they are taken captive' — Jehovah pursues the heart even into exile, into the worst mess a person has made of things. No one is ever too far away for that voice to reach.

POINT 3 — Christians must 'flee from idolatry.' Paul's counsel to the Corinthians is urgent, not casual: 'Therefore, my beloved ones, flee from idolatry.' (1 Cor 10:14) You flee from a fire; you do not stroll away from it while admiring the flames. And idolatry today is rarely a carved figure on a shelf. It is whatever wins our devotion, trust, or fear ahead of Jehovah. The Enjoy Life Forever! book, chapter 54, paragraph 9, reminds us that idolatry takes many forms in our day. Greed and materialism can quietly turn possessions into a way of life — the job, the car, the property that we no longer own but that owns us. Nationalism can demand the kind of total devotion that belongs only to God, which is why we refrain from nationalistic ceremonies — as this meeting's Living as Christians part will consider shortly. Charms, horoscopes, and spiritistic practices bring people into league with demons, not into a relationship with Jehovah. And we can even make idols of people — a preacher, an entertainer, a sports hero, or a beloved human to whom we give the trust and loyalty we owe God alone. Each of those, like the idols in Ezekiel's day, sits down in the sanctuary of the heart.

Here is a simple self-examination, and a hypothetical example to make it concrete. Imagine a sister who realizes she has been checking the news feed, the market, or her favorite team's results first thing every morning — before a word of prayer. Nothing sinful about any single item on that list. But if the first place her heart goes each day belongs to something other than Jehovah, then something has quietly moved into the sanctuary alongside Him. Fleeing from idolatry, in that case, may start with something as small as reversing the order of the first ten minutes of the day. Families can do the same exercise: what gets the best hours of our week? What do we spend on without thinking and sacrifice for without being asked? The answers reveal not what we say we worship but what we actually do. And that is precisely why Paul says flee rather than negotiate: idols rarely leave on their own once they are comfortable.

CONCLUSION: Ezekiel 6 ends on a note of hope. Even in judgment, Jehovah promised: '"'"But I will leave a remnant, for some of you will escape the sword among the nations when you are scattered throughout the lands' (Eze 6:8) He never stops seeking those who will return to him — the whole point of the correction was that his people would 'have to know that I am Jehovah' (Eze 6:10). May nothing in our life ever make our God feel like the betrayed One in that account. Let us keep our worship pure, single-eyed, and reserved for Jehovah — because that is what a heart responsive to him will gladly do.

scriptures.quote: "'Therefore as surely as I am alive,' declares the Sovereign Lord Jehovah, 'because it was my sanctuary that you defiled with all your disgusting idols and with all your detestable practices, I will also reject you; my eye will not feel sorry, and I will show no compassion.

And those who escape will remember me among the nations where they are taken captive. They will realize that I was brokenhearted over their unfaithful heart that turned away from me and at their eyes that are lusting after their disgusting idols. They will be ashamed of and loathe all the evil and detestable things they have done.
"'"But I will leave a remnant, for some of you will escape the sword among the nations when you are scattered throughout the lands.
Therefore, my beloved ones, flee from idolatry.

items.title: Spiritual Gems
items.answer:
What was the significance of Ezekiel's actions at Eze 5:1, 2? Ezekiel shaved his head with a sword and divided the hair into three portions: You will burn a third of it in the fire inside the city when the days of the siege are completed. Then you will take another third and strike it with the sword all around the city, and the last third you will scatter to the wind, and I will draw a sword to chase after them (Eze 5:1, 2) The shaved head pictured humiliation and mourning. Each portion foretold how the inhabitants of Jerusalem would fare: one third dead inside the city during the siege, one third killed by the sword around the city, one third scattered to the wind — and even the scattered ones hunted (Eze 5:12). A few strands tucked in his garment pictured the few who would escape. Ezekiel's strange, painful sign-act made God's warning visible and impossible to forget.

What I learned from this week's Bible reading (Ezekiel 5-6):

1. Our conduct can genuinely wound Jehovah's heart. He told the escapees: 'And those who escape will remember me among the nations where they are taken captive. They will realize that I was brokenhearted over their unfaithful heart that turned away from me and at their eyes that are lusting after their disgusting idols. They will be ashamed of and loathe all the evil and detestable things they have done' (Eze 6:9) Jehovah is not an impersonal force keeping score; he feels the pain of unfaithfulness. That elevates every choice we make from private business to something that touches our God.

2. Even in judgment, Jehovah seeks out the returning ones. '"'"But I will leave a remnant, for some of you will escape the sword among the nations when you are scattered throughout the lands' (Eze 6:8) And why did he preserve them? Not because they were better, but so that they would come to know him: They will have to know that I am Jehovah and that my threats to bring this calamity on them were not empty."' (Eze 6:10) Correction, when Jehovah sends it, is always meant to teach, never merely to punish.

3. Jehovah is not fooled by outward religion. The nation still had a temple, still offered sacrifices — yet their sanctuary was 'defiled' (Eze 5:11). What Jehovah wants is worship that comes from a heart that has turned away from idols, not from a heart that merely keeps up appearances.

Practical examples from these scriptures — how they have helped, or can help:
• Eze 6:9 helped me personally: I was treating a habit of exaggeration at work as harmless 'image management,' until I realized each lie was another object in Jehovah's sanctuary. Naming it as idolatry of self made me finally quit it.
• Eze 6:8 can help a discouraged parent: even when your grown child has wandered far from the truth, Jehovah kept watching over a remnant of escapees in the worst situation imaginable — he can reach your child too, in ways you cannot.
• Eze 6:10 helps in the family: when discipline comes, aim the lesson at knowing Jehovah better, not at shaming — 'they will have to know that I am Jehovah' was the purpose of his correction, and ours should be too.
• And Eze 5:11 warns me before I let anything — money, approval, sport — settle beside Jehovah in my heart. Fleeing early is far easier than excavating later.

scriptures.quote: You will burn a third of it in the fire inside the city when the days of the siege are completed. Then you will take another third and strike it with the sword all around the city, and the last third you will scatter to the wind, and I will draw a sword to chase after them.

And those who escape will remember me among the nations where they are taken captive. They will realize that I was brokenhearted over their unfaithful heart that turned away from me and at their eyes that are lusting after their disgusting idols. They will be ashamed of and loathe all the evil and detestable things they have done.
"'"But I will leave a remnant, for some of you will escape the sword among the nations when you are scattered throughout the lands.
They will have to know that I am Jehovah and that my threats to bring this calamity on them were not empty."'

items.title: Bible Reading — Eze 6:1-10 (th study 5, Accurate Reading)
items.answer:
th study 5, 'Accurate Reading' (Apply Yourself to Reading and Teaching; principle: 1 Timothy 4:13) — read aloud exactly what is on the page.

Context of Eze 6:1-10: Ezekiel, still in Babylon, prophesies against 'the mountains of Israel' — the high places where idol worship had taken root. Jehovah announces that he will destroy the altars and shrines, scatter and slay the people, and leave a remnant who will remember him among the nations and be ashamed of their former idolatry.

Reading tips from the study: prepare well; read in word groupings rather than word by word; observe every punctuation mark, especially the dialogue in verse 9; do not insert, skip, or substitute words; pronounce the names in the passage carefully and naturally.

Possible comment: "'"But I will leave a remnant, for some of you will escape the sword among the nations when you are scattered throughout the lands' (Eze 6:8) Even while announcing destruction on idolatrous Israel, Jehovah promised to leave a remnant. That tells me that no matter how bad things around us get, our God is always looking for the ones who will return to him — so we never let anyone, including ourselves, believe they are beyond his reach.

scriptures.quote: "'"But I will leave a remnant, for some of you will escape the sword among the nations when you are scattered throughout the lands.

items.title: Starting a Conversation — Public Witnessing (lmd lesson 4 point 5)
items.answer:
lmd lesson 4, point 5 — "Remain mild. Do not insist on making a point. We do not want to argue. Show humility by staying calm and knowing when to leave. (Prov. 17:14; Titus 3:2) A mild response may leave the door open for a productive conversation in the future."

PUBLIC WITNESSING — The person wants to argue. Daniel stays calm, offers one mild answer, refuses to insist, and leaves in a way that keeps the door open.

Daniel (Publisher): "Good afternoon, ma'am. We're sharing a Bible-based magazine in the community today. This issue answers the question many people are asking — why God permits suffering."
Ruth (Householder): "A magazine about God? Please. If God cared, my sister would not have died of that illness at 41. Your religion likes to talk while people bury their children!"
Daniel (Publisher): "I'm sorry — losing your sister that young is heavy. And you know, you're not the first person to tell me that what God permits doesn't match what we'd expect of a loving Father."
Ruth (Householder): "Exactly! So what's the point of all this 'good news' you're carrying around?"
Daniel (Publisher): "A fair challenge. The magazine looks at that very question — why a loving God has allowed things to go on like this for so long, and what he has promised to do about it. It helped me a lot when I had a similar question."
Ruth (Householder): "God allowed it — that's what you people say, and then you still praise him! You defend him like a lawyer!"
Daniel (Publisher): "I hear you, and I don't want to turn your doorstep into a debate — that wouldn't help either of us. May I just leave this with you? If the article doesn't satisfy you, then it doesn't. But if you ever want to talk it through, my number is on the back — I'm out here most weekends."
Ruth (Householder): "...Fine, leave it. Don't expect me to agree with it."
Daniel (Publisher): "That's okay. Whatever you conclude, I'm sorry again about your sister. Take care of yourself."

Keys: Daniel carried out lmd lesson 4 point 5 — he remained mild: he acknowledged Ruth's grief instead of defending God the way an argument demands; he did not insist on making his point after she charged him twice; he knew when to leave, following Prov. 17:14 — before the quarrel broke out, he took his leave; and his calm, humble exit left the door open for a productive conversation in the future, exactly as the point promises.

scriptures.quote: Beginning a fight is like opening a floodgate; Before the quarrel breaks out, take your leave.
to speak injuriously of no one, not to be quarrelsome, but to be reasonable, displaying all mildness toward all men.

items.title: Following Up — House to House (lmd lesson 9 point 4)
items.answer:
lmd lesson 9, point 4 — "Think about the interested person. Based on your conversations with him, ask yourself: 'Why does he need to hear the truth?' 'How would studying the Bible make his daily life and his future better?'"

HOUSE TO HOUSE — Daniel returns to a householder he spoke with last month and features a magazine on the topic of their previous conversation, having thought about her real needs.

Daniel (Publisher): "Good morning, Ruth! It's Daniel — we spoke at your door in November. You were telling me about the care home visits to your mother."
Ruth (Householder): "Oh yes, I remember. Come in a moment, the wind is something else today. Yes, Mama is 86 now. Every week it's the same — she forgets more, and I leave there feeling drained."
Daniel (Publisher): "That is a long road, and it does wear on a person. When we spoke, I noticed you asked whether God notices what we go through. So I brought you the magazine I'm featuring this month — its main article is about exactly that: how God feels about the suffering of people he loves, and the hope he holds out for the future — including the promise that our loved ones' minds and bodies will be made whole again."
Ruth (Householder): "Hm. You remembered that? Most people just say, 'Be strong.'"
Daniel (Publisher): "Well, before coming I asked myself two questions: why does Ruth need to hear this truth, and how would the Bible make her daily life better? Your weekly drain, her future, your own tiredness — that's what I had in mind, not just handing out papers."
Ruth (Householder): "And does it really say my mother could get well again?"
Daniel (Publisher): "It says the Bible's hope — the resurrection and perfect health on a paradise earth — reaches even those the world has given up on. May I show you the two paragraphs that carry that promise? It takes two minutes. And if you'd like, we can look at the Bible itself, a small portion at a time, at an hour that suits you — no charge, just questions and answers."
Ruth (Householder): "Mama would like that, actually. She still prays. Come Saturday, around ten."
Daniel (Publisher): "Saturday, ten o'clock. I'll bring the magazine and leave the rest of the world outside the door."

Keys: Daniel carried out lmd lesson 9 point 4 — he thought about the interested person beforehand: why Ruth needs to hear the truth (her draining weekly care of her mother and her unspoken question of whether God cares), and how studying the Bible would make her daily life and future better (a hope that reaches her mother, and comfort that answers her own fatigue). The magazine he featured was on the topic of their previous conversation, and the Bible study offer was shaped to those same needs.

items.title: What Would You Say? — House to House (lmd lesson 1 point 4b)
items.answer: Discussion from the picture (mwb26 November pp. 10-11). Briefly review lmd lesson 1 point 4b — be observant: ask yourself what the person's home tells you about his beliefs or culture — then study the picture with the audience and discuss the two questions beneath it.
items.cite: mwb26 November pp. 10-11 (picture) · lmd lesson 1 point 4b · Psalm 37:29

picture.alt: A house with a beautifully manicured garden
picture.cite: Life and Ministry Meeting Workbook, November 2026 — wol.jw.org

pictureQuestions.label: Question 1
pictureQuestions.q: Based on what you observe, what could you say to start a conversation?
pictureQuestions.answer: Look at the picture first: a cream-painted house, large windows, a warm wooden door — and a garden someone has clearly poured years of love into: a winding flagstone path with moss between the stones, a brilliant red maple, lavender and ferns, rocks set just so, potted plants by the entrance. Not a weed in sight. That is the observation lesson 1 point 4b trains us to make. So you could say: 'Good afternoon! Your garden is beautiful — that red maple, the way the stones line the path. It must take real work. Did you plan it yourself?' Someone who tends a garden like that is proud of it — the compliment is honest, and it starts the conversation on something she cares about.

pictureQuestions.label: Question 2
pictureQuestions.q: Which Bible truth might you share?
pictureQuestions.answer: Her garden shows what we all sense: a beautiful earth that someone with vision and love made enjoyable. That opens the way to the Bible's hope for the whole earth. Tell her that the Bible promises that this love of beauty and order will not stay locked inside our fences — Jehovah purposes to make the entire earth like that garden, a paradise where righteous mankind can build, plant, and enjoy the work of their hands forever, without crime, sickness, or death taking the joy out of it. Somebody who keeps a garden growing through every season already understands the patience that promise requires — and the reward. That truth can lead into a free Bible study.

scriptures.quote: The righteous will possess the earth, And they will live forever on it.

items.title: Why Refrain From Nationalistic Ceremonies?
items.answer:
Sample opening comment: "Jesus refused Satan's offer of 'all the kingdoms of the world,' saying: 'Then Jesus said to him: "Go away, Satan! For it is written: 'It is Jehovah your God you must worship, and it is to him alone you must render sacred service.'' (Matt 4:10) Nationalistic ceremonies — saluting a flag, singing an anthem, pledging allegiance — ask our heart to bow before something other than Jehovah. That is why we refrain from them: not out of disrespect for our neighbours, but out of loyalty to the only One we worship. As you watch the video 'Maintain Neutrality at Public Events,' think about the ceremonies that are common in your own area."

"What good examples can we imitate?" — Sample comment: "The Bible gives us several. Jesus himself kept worship for Jehovah alone, even when the world's rulership was offered to him. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refused to bow to the image Nebuchadnezzar set up, even with the furnace in front of them. And Daniel kept praying to Jehovah as he had always done, though a law forbade it. The video adds modern examples — publishers our own age, who quietly but firmly did not salute a flag or stand for an anthem, yet stayed respectful while doing it. What stands out in all of them is the combination: firmness toward God, courtesy toward people."

"How can families prepare so that they are not caught off guard?" — Sample comment: "Preparation starts at home, long before the school assembly or the stadium. Parents can rehearse with their children what they will do and say — just as this meeting is doing. A young person needs to know why we refrain, in his own words, not just that we do. Decide the respectful way to decline in advance: 'I respect the country, but as one of Jehovah's Witnesses I don't participate in salutes to flags or anthems.' Families can also anticipate the usual moments — the first day of school, national holidays, civic events, the workplace ceremony — so the moment of decision arrives already decided. And when a young one has taken a stand, parents should be ready to speak with teachers or officials calmly and to follow up with warm commendation at home."

"What helpful information have you found from the organization on this subject?" — Sample comment: "The jw.org website carries a whole section on neutrality, including the video series for young people about taking stands at school, experiences of Witnesses around the world who remained neutral under pressure, and articles explaining why Jehovah's Witnesses do not salute the flag or sing nationalistic songs. The book God's Kingdom Rules discusses our neutrality in detail, and the brochures and chapters we study — including this meeting's discussion — keep the subject fresh. The practical tip many of us have used: read those experiences to your children, not to frighten them but to show them that thousands of brothers and sisters have stood the same test and Jehovah carried them through."

scriptures.quote: Then Jesus said to him: "Go away, Satan! For it is written: 'It is Jehovah your God you must worship, and it is to him alone you must render sacred service.'"

items.cite: Mt 4:10; video 'Maintain Neutrality at Public Events'

items.title: Congregation Bible Study — A Boy Who Spoke Up for Jehovah (wcg chap. 21)
items.answer: Study source: the book Walk Courageously With God! (wcg), chapter 21, "A Boy Who Spoke Up for Jehovah" — the account of young Samuel at Shiloh (wcg chap. 21 pp. 98-101). The Bible account read: 1 Samuel 1:9-11, 24-28; 2:12-36; 3:1-21; 25:1; Hebrews 11:32. Below are prepared answers to every question in the chapter — the discussion question, Dig Deeper, Reflect on the Lessons and Meditate on the Bigger Picture.

cbs.label: For discussion
cbs.q: In what ways did Samuel show courage?
cbs.answer: Samuel showed courage in several ways. He had to deliver Jehovah's judgment message to Eli — the high priest, the nation's spiritual leader, a man he had served since childhood — knowing the news was all bad. The chapter says he was 'afraid to tell Eʹli of the vision,' yet 'Samuel told him everything.' (1 Sam 3:15) He showed courage too by growing up pure amid corruption: Hophni and Phinehas were defiling the tabernacle right around him, and that environment did not swallow him. And he kept the courage his whole life as prophet and judge. Courage began for Samuel as a boy choosing Jehovah's side when it was costly to do so.

scriptures.quote: Samuel lay down until the morning; then he opened the doors of Jehovah's house. Samuel was afraid to tell Eʹli of the vision.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 1
cbs.q: Describe Shiloh, the site of Jehovah's tabernacle. (w92 11/1 8-9)
cbs.answer: Shiloh sat in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Jerusalem — after the land was subdued, the tent of meeting was set up there, and for some three centuries it remained Israel's center of worship; the whole nation traveled there for the yearly festivals. The chapter's picture A shows the site today: a bare, windswept hilltop with only traces of ancient ruins — no temple, no monument, nothing grand. That is a lesson in itself: pure worship never depended on impressive buildings. A tent in the hills housed the worship of Jehovah's chosen nation. What made Shiloh precious was not architecture but the presence of Jehovah's arrangement there.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 2
cbs.q: What was life like for Samuel at the tabernacle? (ia 60-62 ¶9-13)
cbs.answer: It was a life of humble service and simple routines. As a small boy Samuel 'became a minister of Jehovah before Eʹli the priest' (1 Sam 2:11). His family visited once a year — his mother brought him a little sleeveless coat she had made (1 Sam 2:19) — so home was a memory he carried through the year. He grew up under elderly, nearly blind Eli while Hophni and Phinehas disgraced the priesthood around him. Yet the record says: 'Meanwhile, the boy Samuel kept growing in stature and in favor both with Jehovah and with the people.' (1 Sam 2:26) Service there was far from ideal circumstances — but it trained a prophet.

scriptures.quote: Also, his mother would make for him a little sleeveless coat, and she brought it up to him year after year when she came up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.
Meanwhile, the boy Samuel kept growing in stature and in favor both with Jehovah and with the people.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 3
cbs.q: In what sense had young Samuel 'not yet come to know Jehovah'? (1 Sam 3:7; w02 12/15 8 ¶5-6)
cbs.answer: The account explains itself: 'Now Samuel had not yet come to know Jehovah, and the word of Jehovah had not yet been revealed to him.' (1 Sam 3:7) Samuel already served, already believed — but knowing Jehovah here means personal, firsthand experience of him. The boy had heard about Jehovah; he had not yet received his own word from him, nor seen how Jehovah acts on those who serve him. That comes only with time and experience. So a young person can love Jehovah sincerely and still be 'coming to know' him — every answered prayer, every trial endured with his help, deepens that knowledge into friendship.

scriptures.quote: Now Samuel had not yet come to know Jehovah, and the word of Jehovah had not yet been revealed to him.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 4
cbs.q: How was the prophecy regarding Eli's family fulfilled? (it "Eli, I" ¶5-7)
cbs.answer: Jehovah said through the man of God: 'Look! Days are coming when I will cut off your strength and that of your father's house, so that no man in your house will live to old age.' (1 Sam 2:31) It happened exactly. Hophni and Phinehas died the same day in battle with the Philistines; when Eli heard that the ark had been captured, he fell and died. The word continued to work through Samuel's own prophecy. And the priesthood itself later passed from Eli's line to Zadok, fulfilling the promise that a faithful priest would act in harmony with Jehovah's heart. Nothing Jehovah foretold about that house was left unfulfilled.

scriptures.quote: Look! Days are coming when I will cut off your strength and that of your father's house, so that no man in your house will live to old age.

cbs.label: Reflect · 1
cbs.q: What can a young person learn from Samuel about the importance of being eager to obey? (1 Sam 3:5)
cbs.answer: Samuel did not answer the call on the fourth try — he answered every time. 'Here I am, for you called me.' (1 Sam 3:5) Three times he got up in the dark, ran to Eli, and three times was sent back to bed — and he still got up again instantly. Eagerness in obedience means there is no delay, no 'in a minute,' no grumbling about being disturbed. A young person who learns to respond quickly to direction from parents, elders, and above all Jehovah builds the habit that made Samuel usable: when the real call came, the reflex was already there.

scriptures.quote: He ran to Eʹli and said: "Here I am, for you called me." But he said: "I did not call. Lie down again." So he went and lay down.

cbs.label: Reflect · 2
cbs.q: What can a young person learn about being polite and respectful? (1 Sam 3:6-10)
cbs.answer: Being sent back three times could have made a boy sulky — Samuel stayed respectful through all of it, addressing Eli properly and accepting the correction each time. Then, when he finally recognized who was calling, he answered exactly as Eli had taught him: 'Speak, for your servant is listening.' (1 Sam 3:10) Respectful means listening fully before you speak — 'for your servant is listening' came before any request of his own. Young ones today can imitate that: receive instructions without eye-rolling or arguing, answer politely even when disappointed, and give elders and parents the honor of a genuinely attentive ear.

scriptures.quote: Jehovah came and stood there, and he called as at the other times: "Samuel, Samuel!" At this Samuel said: "Speak, for your servant is listening."

cbs.label: Reflect · 3
cbs.q: What can a young person learn about being dependable? (1 Sam 3:15)
cbs.answer: Samuel had just spent a terrifying night, and by dawn he still had a job to do: 'Samuel lay down until the morning; then he opened the doors of Jehovah's house.' (1 Sam 3:15) He was afraid to tell Eli of the vision — yet he did not hide, he did not skip his duties, and he did not make his fear other people's problem. Dependability means others can count on you to do your part even on your worst day. A young person dependable in small things — chores, assignments, being where he said he would be — is being prepared for weightier service, just as Samuel was.

scriptures.quote: Samuel lay down until the morning; then he opened the doors of Jehovah's house. Samuel was afraid to tell Eʹli of the vision.

cbs.label: Reflect · 4
cbs.q: When might a young person need to speak up, and how can the example of Samuel help him?
cbs.answer: A young person may need to speak up when schoolmates invite him to cheat, use drugs, or view pornography; when a teacher insists he salute the flag or join a patriotic ceremony; when relatives press him to celebrate a holiday he does not share; or when he sees another child being bullied. Samuel's example helps in three ways. First, deliver the message — however hard the audience: he 'told him everything' even though Eli was the high priest. Second, be respectful while being firm, as Samuel always was with Eli. Third, trust that Jehovah stands behind the one who speaks for him: 'Jehovah himself was with him' as Samuel grew (1 Sam 3:19).

scriptures.quote: Samuel continued growing up, and Jehovah himself was with him and did not let any of all his words go unfulfilled.

cbs.label: Reflect · 5
cbs.q: In what other ways might you imitate the courage of Samuel?
cbs.answer: Courage to keep worship pure when the environment is corrupt — like Samuel, who stayed clean while Hophni and Phinehas defiled the tabernacle around him. Courage to accept a hard assignment from Jehovah without arguing — Samuel had to announce judgment on the man who had raised him. Courage to remain humble when used in a big way: Jehovah made the boy's words count, and Samuel did not let it spoil him. And courage to grow old in faithful service — he kept it for decades, not just one dramatic night. For all of us, adult or young: serve where you are planted, speak when Jehovah's name is at stake, and never stop.

cbs.label: Meditate · A
cbs.q: What does this account teach me about Jehovah?
cbs.answer: It teaches me that Jehovah does not show favoritism for position: the high priest's corrupt house fell, while a small boy serving in the same courtyard became his spokesman. It teaches me that Jehovah sees individuals in corrupt environments — he watched Samuel grow in favor there, and he watches us. It teaches me that his word, once spoken, never fails: 'he did not let any of all [Samuel's] words go unfulfilled.' (1 Sam 3:19) And it teaches me that Jehovah draws close to the humble: he came and stood and called a child by name — twice — to make sure the boy knew who was speaking.

scriptures.quote: Samuel continued growing up, and Jehovah himself was with him and did not let any of all his words go unfulfilled.

cbs.label: Meditate · B
cbs.q: How does the account tie in with Jehovah's purposes?
cbs.answer: Samuel stands at a hinge of Bible history: the last of the judges and the prophet who anointed the first kings, through whom Jehovah organized his people around the royal line that would produce the Messiah. His faithfulness preserved pure worship at the moment it was nearly destroyed by a corrupt priesthood, and God's promise that 'a faithful priest' would walk before His anointed one looked ahead to Jesus Christ, the ultimate faithful High Priest. Samuel is also named among the faith-keeping men and women of Hebrews 11 — proof that even a child's courage becomes part of the story Jehovah is telling about the Seed and the Kingdom.

cbs.label: Meditate · C
cbs.q: What would I like to ask Samuel in the resurrection?
cbs.answer: I would love to ask him: 'What went through your mind that fourth time you lay down and heard your name called — were you afraid it was Eli again?' And: 'When you told Eli the judgment, did you watch for his reaction, or did you look away?' I would also like to ask about his mother — did he really remember Hannah's coat from when he was three? And what it felt like, decades later, to anoint Saul and then David, knowing the future of a nation was passing through his hands. I suspect he would answer, as always, by pointing back to Jehovah: 'Speak — your servant is listening.'

wt.article: Treasure Your Share in Modern-Day Miracles

items.q: (a) What are some miracles that are recorded in the Bible? (b) What is a miracle, and what part can we play? (1 Cor 3:9)
items.comment: I can picture standing by the Red Sea watching the waters pile up, or seeing Jesus call a dead man out of a tomb — Matthew 15:31 says the crowds glorified the God of Israel when they saw such things. But a miracle is simply something beyond man's ability to accomplish or even fully understand — something only Jehovah can bring about by his power. And here is the thrilling part: the article says three miracles of that kind are happening inside Jehovah's organization right now. We are not asked to watch them — we get to be 'fellow workers' with Jehovah as he performs them (1 Cor 3:9).

scriptures.quote: For we are God's fellow workers. You are God's field under cultivation, God's building.
scriptures.use: Identifies our privilege of being 'fellow workers' with Jehovah as he accomplishes modern-day miracles.

scriptures.quote: So the crowd felt amazement as they saw the speechless speaking and the maimed being made sound and the lame walking and the blind seeing, and they glorified the God of Israel.
scriptures.use: Shows the response of any righteous-hearted person who witnessed Bible-era miracles — no doubt that God was behind them.

items.insight: The definition does the work: a miracle is what man cannot do, so growth, unity and love in this organization cannot be explained by man — which is exactly what their opposers keep being forced to admit.
items.apply: Pick one of the three miracles — growth, unity, love — and this week do one deliberate thing to work alongside Jehovah in it, instead of just admiring it.

paraNotes.points: Bible miracles — the Red Sea, Jesus' cures and resurrections — left witnesses with no doubt God was behind them (Matt 15:31).
paraNotes.highlight: The question hangs over the article from the start: are miracles happening today? Yes.

paraNotes.points: A miracle = something beyond man's ability to accomplish or understand fully, brought about by Jehovah's power; the article will examine three happening today.
paraNotes.highlight: Each of us can be a 'fellow worker' with Jehovah in them — that is the article's whole focus (1 Cor 3:9).

items.q: Why can it be said that Jehovah's people have become “a mighty nation”? (Isaiah 60:22) (See also picture.)
items.comment: Isaiah foretold it: 'The little one will become a thousand And the small one a mighty nation. I myself, Jehovah, will speed it up in its own time.' (Isa 60:22) In 1914 those serving Jehovah were about 5,000. Today they are over nine million evangelizers in 240 lands — more than the population of 130 countries. And the growth is not organizational padding: no infant baptism, no lowered standards — people studied, changed their lives, qualified, dedicated themselves and got baptized. That is why 'the small one' can honestly be called 'a mighty nation.'

scriptures.quote: The little one will become a thousand And the small one a mighty nation. I myself, Jehovah, will speed it up in its own time.
scriptures.use: The prophecy whose fulfillment makes Jehovah's people a 'mighty nation,' which Jehovah himself speeds up.

items.insight: The arithmetic is the argument: 5,000 in 1914 to over nine million in 240 lands — 'the little one... a thousand.' Growth of that shape and speed is the miracle Isaiah named.
items.apply: Tell someone this week the 1914 figure — 5,000 — before you show today's number; the contrast is what makes the growth miraculous.

paraNotes.points: Isa 60:22 foretold the increase: from about 5,000 in 1914 to over nine million Kingdom evangelizers in 240 lands.
paraNotes.highlight: Study the picture with this paragraph — the worldwide increase in one lifetime.

items.q: Why is this growth in numbers significant?
items.comment: Because of how the number was built. Many religions count babies as members; we do not. And nobody relaxed God's moral standards to make the statistics look good — quite the reverse: each one of us studied the Bible and brought our life into harmony with it, which for many meant real changes in thinking and conduct (1 Cor 6:9-11). Then came qualifying as publishers, then dedication, then baptism (Matt 28:19, 20). So every one of those nine million is a person who paid something to be there. That is what makes the number significant — and miraculous.

scriptures.quote: And yet that is what some of you were. But you have been washed clean; you have been sanctified; you have been declared righteous in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and with the spirit of our God.
scriptures.use: Many of us were once among 'some of you were' — washed clean, sanctified, declared righteous after real changes in conduct.

scriptures.quote: Go, therefore, and make disciples of people of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the holy spirit, 20 teaching them to observe all the things I have commanded you. And look! I am with you all the days until the conclusion of the system of things."
scriptures.use: The disciple-making and baptizing work through which each of the nine million actually entered true worship.

items.insight: The growth is quality-checked at every step — study, change, qualify, dedicate, baptize. A 'mighty nation' built that way cannot be explained as organizational enthusiasm.
items.apply: Recall what it personally cost you to become one of that number — and tell that story to someone who is now paying their own price.

paraNotes.points: No infant baptism, no relaxed moral standards: individuals studied, changed their conduct (1 Cor 6:9-11), qualified as publishers, dedicated themselves and got baptized.
paraNotes.highlight: Every number in that nine million represents a life that was deliberately changed.

items.q: What did Jesus tell his followers to expect?
items.comment: Trouble, not applause. Jesus said: 'If anyone wants to come after me, let him disown himself and pick up his torture stake and keep following me.' (Matt 16:24) His followers would be willing to suffer, even to die. He foretold trials before governors and kings (Matt 10:17, 18), opposition from powerful religious authorities (John 16:2), and division even inside families because of pure worship (Matt 10:34-36). So a disciple of Christ never signed up for an easy road — which is all the more reason that nine million people on that road is a miracle.

scriptures.quote: Then Jesus said to his disciples: "If anyone wants to come after me, let him disown himself and pick up his torture stake and keep following me.
scriptures.use: Jesus' own description of what becoming his follower would cost — self-sacrifice, even suffering.

items.insight: Jesus never marketed discipleship as safe. The fact that millions still line up for the 'torture stake' road proves something outside human persuasion is at work.
items.apply: Whatever your hardest consequence of following Jesus is, name it to Jehovah in prayer today — not to be released from it, but to be strengthened in it.

paraNotes.points: Jesus said following him means self-sacrifice (Matt 16:24), possibly suffering or death; he foretold trials before governors and kings, religious opposition, and family division.
paraNotes.highlight: The word 'torture stake' keeps the cost before our eyes — Christianity was never presented as comfortable.

items.q: Why could opposers not overthrow the first-century Christians?
items.comment: The Sanhedrin wanted to 'do away with' the apostles, but Gamaliel gave the Jewish court advice he probably didn't realize was prophetic: 'Do not meddle with these men, but let them alone. For if this scheme or this work is from men, it will be overthrown; but if it is from God, you will not be able to overthrow them.' (Acts 5:38, 39) And that proved to be exactly the test result. The persecution continued, but 'the word of God continued to spread' (Acts 6:7). The reason was never organizational strength — God was helping his people endure and grow (Acts 1:8).

scriptures.quote: So under the present circumstances, I say to you, do not meddle with these men, but let them alone. For if this scheme or this work is from men, it will be overthrown; 39 but if it is from God, you will not be able to overthrow them. Otherwise, you may even be found fighters against God himself."
scriptures.use: Gamaliel's caution to the Sanhedrin — the work would collapse if it were of men.

scriptures.quote: but if it is from God, you will not be able to overthrow them. Otherwise, you may even be found fighters against God himself."
scriptures.use: The other half of the test: if the work is from God, it cannot be overthrown — and it was not.

scriptures.quote: Consequently, the word of God continued to spread, and the number of the disciples kept multiplying very much in Jerusalem; and a large crowd of priests began to be obedient to the faith.
scriptures.use: The result after the apostles' release: opposition failed to stop the spreading of the word.

scriptures.quote: But you will receive power when the holy spirit comes upon you, and you will be witnesses of me in Jerusalem, in all Ju·deʹa and Sa·marʹi·a, and to the most distant part of the earth."
scriptures.use: The power behind Christian witnessing that persecution could not cancel.

items.insight: Gamaliel's logic is still the sharpest argument in our defense: every human movement that is persecuted dies — unless God is in it. Ours has been persecuted for a century and keeps growing.
items.apply: When opposition or ridicule makes you feel small, remember you are on the side that Gamaliel's own test has already vindicated.

paraNotes.points: The Sanhedrin tried to stop the apostles; Gamaliel cautioned against fighting God (Acts 5:33, 34, 38, 39); the word kept spreading (Acts 6:7) because God was helping his people (Acts 1:8).
paraNotes.highlight: Gamaliel 'may not have realized how true his words were' — an enemy of the work supplied its best accreditation.

items.q: How are Jesus' disciples today following the example of the first-century Christians? (See also the box “Growth Despite Persecution.”)
items.comment: Thousands today are accepting the truth knowing exactly what it will cost them — family rejection, being disowned, even violence. Why would anyone do that? Love for Jehovah and trust in his care. He gives them 'the power beyond what is normal' to endure (2 Cor 4:7-9), and those disowned by family can pray with the psalmist: 'Even if my own father and mother abandon me, Jehovah himself will take me in.' (Ps 27:10) The box drives it home: in the Netherlands, under Nazi occupation, publishers rose 115 percent in two years. Persecution has never once stopped this work.

scriptures.quote: However, we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the power beyond what is normal may be God's and not from us.
scriptures.use: The 'power beyond what is normal' Jehovah gives persecuted disciples to endure.

scriptures.quote: Even if my own father and mother abandon me, Jehovah himself will take me in.
scriptures.use: The consolation of those rejected or disowned by family for their faith.

items.insight: The box is the control experiment: when the cost of joining rises sharply, human movements shrink. The Witnesses grew 115 percent. That is the fingerprint of divine backing.
items.apply: If you know a brother or sister who was disowned for the truth, reach out to them this week — be one of the ways Jehovah 'takes them in.'

paraNotes.points: Thousands flock to the truth despite rejection, disowning and persecution, out of love for Jehovah (Matt 16:24); he gives them power beyond what is normal (2 Cor 4:7-9).
paraNotes.highlight: Box 'Growth Despite Persecution': in WWII the Netherlands' publishers rose 115 percent in two years — 'The more you persecute the Witnesses the more they grow.'

items.q: What share do we have in the miracle of growth?
items.comment: Every time we engage in the ministry in any form, we are working alongside Jehovah and Jesus in the miracle of growth. Jesus' own promise makes that a working arrangement, not a slogan: 'I am with you all the days until the conclusion of the system of things.' (Matt 28:20) And we are assisted by the angels as we preach (Rev 14:6, 7). So when I place a tract, make a return visit, or support the cart work, I am not decorating a statistic — I am one of the hands by which 'the small one' became 'a mighty nation.'

scriptures.quote: teaching them to observe all the things I have commanded you. And look! I am with you all the days until the conclusion of the system of things."
scriptures.use: Jesus' assurance of his support 'all the days' — the backing behind our share in the growth.

scriptures.quote: And I saw another angel flying in midheaven, and he had everlasting good news to declare to those who dwell on the earth, to every nation and tribe and tongue and people.
scriptures.use: The angelic direction and assistance under which the preaching work is carried out.

items.insight: Our share is not optional decoration: 'fellow workers' means the miracle is accomplished partly through us — which also means every form of the ministry counts, not just the impressive ones.
items.apply: Schedule one extra ministry segment this week and consciously do it 'alongside Jehovah' — praying before, not just after.

paraNotes.points: In any form of the ministry we work alongside Jehovah and Jesus (Matt 28:20), assisted by the angels (Rev 14:6, 7).
paraNotes.highlight: 'I am with you all the days' — the Master's presence is the constant, whatever the day's results.

items.q: How is Micah 2:12 being fulfilled today?
items.comment: Micah foretold a second miracle: 'I will certainly gather all of you, O Jacob; I will surely collect the remaining ones of Israel together. In unity I will place them, like sheep in the pen…' (Mic 2:12) God's people today live in harmony despite differences of personality and background — David's words are our experience: 'Look! How good and how pleasant it is For brothers to dwell together in unity!' (Ps 133:1) Wherever we go, the same spiritual program at meetings, assemblies and conventions; brothers from every background working side by side on building projects and at Bethel. Our loving family is there for us anywhere on earth.

scriptures.quote: I will certainly gather all of you, O Jacob; I will surely collect the remaining ones of Israel together. In unity I will place them, like sheep in the pen, Like a flock in its pasture; It will be noisy with people.'
scriptures.use: The prophecy of Jehovah gathering his people and placing them together in unity.

scriptures.quote: Look! How good and how pleasant it is For brothers to dwell together in unity!
scriptures.use: The psalm that describes the pleasantness of that brotherly unity, which God's people today experience.

items.insight: Unity here is not similarity — the miracle is harmony despite differences of personality and background, not the absence of them.
items.apply: Next meeting, deliberately sit with and greet someone whose background or age is nothing like yours — that pen holds many kinds of sheep.

paraNotes.points: Micah foretold the gathering of God's people to dwell together in unity (Mic 2:12); David's psalm describes it (Ps 133:1).
paraNotes.highlight: The unity exists despite differences in personality and background — that is what makes it a miracle rather than a club.

paraNotes.points: Same spiritual program worldwide at meetings, assemblies, conventions; Witnesses of all backgrounds work side by side on builds and at Bethel; the family is there for us wherever we go.
paraNotes.highlight: 'Never before in history have so many people from so many lands and cultures been united in thought and in conduct.'

items.q: Why can our unity be called a miracle?
items.comment: Because of the contrast. The world around us is coming apart — the news is nothing but fights, riots, protests, rebellions and wars, and it matches Bible prophecy about the last days: 'betrayers, headstrong, puffed up with pride' (2 Tim 3:4). Meanwhile 'the whole world is lying in the power of the wicked one' (1 John 5:19) — and Satan is actively trying to divide us (Rev 12:9). With the whole planet's atmosphere pushing toward disunity, for millions of different people to remain united in thought and conduct cannot be humanly engineered. It is miraculous.

scriptures.quote: betrayers, headstrong, puffed up with pride, lovers of pleasures rather than lovers of God,
scriptures.use: Paul's prophecy of the divisive traits that mark the last days — the very atmosphere our unity defies.

scriptures.quote: We know that we originate with God, but the whole world is lying in the power of the wicked one.
scriptures.use: The world lies in the power of the wicked one — yet God's people thrive united in it.

items.insight: Unity in a divided world is not just nice — it is evidence. It is what the 'mighty nation' looks like from the inside: the same miracle, viewed from a different angle.
items.apply: When the news fills you with the world's division, counter it deliberately with something from our worldwide brotherhood — a report, a letter, a call to a distant congregation.

paraNotes.points: Our unity is in striking contrast to the world's disunity — fights, riots, wars — as prophesied (2 Tim 3:2-4); despite Satan's control of the world (1 John 5:19; Rev 12:9) we thrive as a united people.
paraNotes.highlight: The wicked one works to divide — a united family inside his domain is a standing refutation of him.

items.q: How can we contribute to the bond of unity among God's people?
items.comment: By listening to and applying what Jehovah teaches us. His Word teaches patience, forgiveness, avoiding arguments, kindness (Eph 4:2, 31, 32). So the contribution is small and repeated: each time I overlook a flaw in a brother, each time I refuse to pass on the juicy piece of news, each time I extend forgiveness when I have a right to be offended — right there, I am working along with Jehovah on a modern-day miracle. Unity is not maintained in grand decisions; it is maintained in exactly those daily choices.

scriptures.quote: with all humility and mildness, with patience, putting up with one another in love,
scriptures.use: The attitudes Paul lists as the engine of unity — humility, mildness, patience, forbearance in love.

scriptures.quote: But become kind to one another, tenderly compassionate, freely forgiving one another just as God also by Christ freely forgave you.
scriptures.use: Kindness, tender compassion and free forgiveness — the daily actions that contribute to the bond.

items.insight: Notice the scale of the assignment: not 'fix the organization's unity' but 'overlook one flaw, control one urge, forgive one offense' — the miracle is built from grains.
items.apply: Choose one person you have been keeping a small grievance against, and bury it this week — genuinely, not passively.

paraNotes.points: Contribute by listening to and applying what Jehovah teaches — patience, forgiveness, avoiding arguments, kindness (Eph 4:2, 31, 32).
paraNotes.highlight: Each overlooked flaw and each controlled urge to gossip is presented as literally working with Jehovah on a miracle.

items.q: In what ways did first-century Christians show love for one another? (John 13:35)
items.comment: Jesus made love the identity card of his disciples: 'By this all will know that you are my disciples—if you have love among yourselves.' (John 13:35) And the first century lived up to it: they shared their belongings with those in need (Acts 2:44, 45), they prayed and fought for the persecuted (Acts 12:5), they cared for orphans and widows (Jas 1:27), and although many were poor themselves, they sent relief aid to brothers far away (2 Cor 8:1-4). Even outsiders noticed — Tertullian quoted them saying, 'See... how they love one another.'

scriptures.quote: By this all will know that you are my disciples—if you have love among yourselves."
scriptures.use: Jesus' statement that love among disciples is the identifying mark.

scriptures.quote: All those who became believers were together and had everything in common, 45 and they were selling their possessions and properties and distributing the proceeds to all, according to what each one needed.
scriptures.use: First-century Christians shared belongings with those in need.

scriptures.quote: and they were selling their possessions and properties and distributing the proceeds to all, according to what each one needed.
scriptures.use: They sold possessions to distribute proceeds to each according to need.

scriptures.quote: So Peter was being kept in the prison, but the congregation was intensely praying to God for him.
scriptures.use: The congregation intensely praying for the persecuted Peter — support for the persecuted.

scriptures.quote: The form of worship that is clean and undefiled from the standpoint of our God and Father is this: to look after orphans and widows in their tribulation, and to keep oneself without spot from the world.
scriptures.use: Looking after orphans and widows as part of clean worship.

items.insight: Love was expressed through concrete redistribution — property, prayer, orphan care, famine relief — not through sentiment. Tertullian's outsiders saw deeds, not slogans.
items.apply: Identify one practical need in the congregation this week — a meal, a ride, a visit — and meet it without being asked.

paraNotes.points: First-century love was central: sharing belongings (Acts 2:44, 45), supporting the persecuted (Acts 12:5), caring for orphans and widows (Jas 1:27), sending relief aid despite poverty (2 Cor 8:1-4).
paraNotes.highlight: Tertullian's quote — 'See... how they love one another' — came from outside observers, not from Christians themselves.

items.q: In what ways do God's people show love today? (See also pictures.)
items.comment: The same love, modern form. We extend it beyond the congregation through the preaching work, supporting it financially — freely, with no begging, no tithing. We help brothers materially in disasters. And we carry one another emotionally and spiritually, just as Paul urged: 'Speak consolingly to those who are depressed, support the weak, be patient toward all.' (1 Thess 5:14) Jehovah has brought us into a worldwide family where love is not an idea we defend but a life we live — pictures in this article show it in action.

scriptures.quote: On the other hand, we urge you, brothers, to warn the disorderly, speak consolingly to those who are depressed, support the weak, be patient toward all.
scriptures.use: Paul's admonition that shapes the congregation's spiritual and emotional support today.

items.insight: Support is three-stranded — material, spiritual, emotional. A congregation strong in only one strand has not yet shown the love the article is describing.
items.apply: Think of the most discouraged person you know in the congregation, and speak one consoling, specific sentence to them this week.

paraNotes.points: Love today: preaching to those outside, voluntary financial support with no tithing, material disaster relief, and spiritual/emotional support (1 Thess 5:14).
paraNotes.highlight: Footnote a points to the jw.org article on 2023 disaster relief — 'We See Firsthand Jehovah's Love' — a recent, documented example.

items.q: Why can our love for one another be called a miracle?
items.comment: Because of where it is growing. Paul prophesied that people would be 'lovers of themselves, lovers of money,' lovers of pleasures rather than lovers of God, and 'having no natural affection' — not even for their own family (2 Tim 3:2-4). Jesus said love would cool off in the greater number (Matt 24:10, 12). Look around: that is exactly the world we live in, and we are not immune to its air. Yet in that climate, millions of people keep loving — patiently, sacrificially, across every division. Love that thrives in a loveless world is not a temperament. It is the result of Jehovah's power.

scriptures.quote: For men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, haughty, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, disloyal, 3 having no natural affection, not open to any agreement, slanderers, without self-control, fierce, without love of goodness, 4 betrayers, headstrong, puffed up with pride, lovers of pleasures rather than lovers of God, 5 having an appearance of godliness but proving false to its power; and from these turn away.
scriptures.use: Paul's prophecy of the self-love of the last days — the climate our love grows against.

scriptures.quote: Then, too, many will be stumbled and will betray one another and will hate one another.
scriptures.use: Jesus' foretelling of betrayal and hatred — the cooling of love foretold for the last days.

scriptures.quote: and because of the increasing of lawlessness, the love of the greater number will grow cold.
scriptures.use: The love of the greater number grows cold — yet God's people's love is kept warm.

items.insight: Love surviving 'the love of the greater number grow[ing] cold' is the negative-space proof of the miracle: what should have cooled, did not — in us.
items.apply: Name one relationship where your love has cooled recently, and do one warm thing about it this week before it cools further.

paraNotes.points: Our love is miraculous because it thrives in a selfish world prophesied to be 'lovers of themselves' with 'no natural affection' (2 Tim 3:2-4) and cooling love (Matt 24:10, 12).
paraNotes.highlight: 'Have you not found this to be true as you observe the state of this world?' — the article makes each of us the witness.

items.q: In what ways can we show love to one another?
items.comment: In ways that are almost embarrassingly ordinary. We show love when we sincerely express appreciation to others for their good example, and when we work to maintain peace with them (Mark 9:50). Notice that the article does not say 'when we feel loving' — it says demonstrating love consistently, in words and in actions. Say the thank-you out loud. Make the peace-seeking phone call first. Be the one who will not let a division in the congregation harden. That everyday consistency is how we reflect the quality that identifies God's people.

scriptures.quote: Salt is fine, but if the salt ever loses its saltiness, with what will you season it? Have salt in yourselves, and keep peace with one another."
scriptures.use: Jesus' 'have salt in yourselves and keep peace with one another' — maintaining peace as an expression of love.

items.insight: Appreciation and peacemaking are named, not grand gestures: love is proven mostly by what we say out loud and what we refuse to escalate.
items.apply: This week, commend one person for their good example — by name, specifically, and preferably in front of others.

paraNotes.points: Show love by sincerely expressing appreciation for others' good example and by working to maintain peace (Mark 9:50), in words and actions.
paraNotes.highlight: Consistency is the test — 'consistently demonstrating love in both words and actions' reflects the identifying quality.

items.q: What proves to you that Jehovah is performing miracles today?
items.comment: Three lines of evidence, all running at once. In the face of widespread opposition, our numbers increased. In a world splintered on every level, we are united. And in a loveless world, our love for God and for one another identifies us as true disciples (John 13:34). None of those trends exists anywhere else on earth — and we are not passive bystanders to them: 'we are God's fellow workers' (1 Cor 3:9). Personally, what proves it to me is that I have watched all three miracles continue through years when it would have been easy for any one of them to fail.

scriptures.quote: I am giving you a new commandment, that you love one another; just as I have loved you, you also love one another.
scriptures.use: Jesus' new commandment — the love that identifies true disciples in a loveless world.

scriptures.quote: For we are God's fellow workers. You are God's field under cultivation, God's building.
scriptures.use: Our standing as God's fellow workers, not passive bystanders to the miracles.

items.insight: The three miracles are the article's own syllogism: opposition couldn't shrink us, division couldn't split us, lovelessness couldn't freeze us — therefore Jehovah.
items.apply: Write down one sentence — for your own eyes — about which of the three miracles you have personally seen Jehovah perform in your years in the truth.

paraNotes.points: Growth despite opposition, unity in a splintered world, love in a loveless world (John 13:34) — the three together prove Jehovah is performing miracles now.
paraNotes.highlight: 'We are not passive bystanders' — the conclusion reassigns us from audience to participants (1 Cor 3:9).

items.q: In view of the miraculous work that Jehovah is doing, what determination should we have?
items.comment: To treasure our privilege — always. Think of what we are seeing: people from all lands enjoying growth, unity and love in a world that has none of the three. These miracles are not just present blessings; they strengthen our confidence that everything else Jehovah has promised is coming too — 'new heavens and a new earth that we are awaiting according to his promise' (2 Pet 3:13). So the determination: never treat my share in this work as routine. Every meeting attended, every call made, every act of love is a share in a miracle no generation before ours has witnessed.

scriptures.quote: But there are new heavens and a new earth that we are awaiting according to his promise, and in these righteousness is to dwell.
scriptures.use: The promise the present miracles strengthen our confidence in — new heavens and a new earth.

items.insight: The miracles are down payments: their fulfillment today is the evidence clause for every remaining promise of Jehovah, including the new world.
items.apply: End each day this week by naming one way you shared in a miracle that day — and let that habit reset how you see 'routine' theocracy.

paraNotes.points: Growth, unity and love amid a troubled world strengthen confidence in all Jehovah's promises (2 Pet 3:13).
paraNotes.highlight: The closing charge is for every one of us: 'Always treasure your privilege to have a share in God's modern-day miracles.'

recap.q: How can we contribute to the miracle of growth?
recap.comment: By engaging in the ministry in any form — every tract placed, return visit made and conversation started is working alongside Jehovah and Jesus in the growth, with Jesus' assurance 'I am with you all the days' and the angels' assistance.

recap.q: How can we contribute to the miracle of unity?
recap.comment: By carefully listening to and applying what Jehovah teaches: showing patience, extending forgiveness, avoiding arguments, overlooking flaws, controlling the urge to gossip, and being kind — each such choice is working with Jehovah on the bond of unity.

recap.q: How can we contribute to the miracle of love?
recap.comment: By sincerely expressing appreciation for others' good example, maintaining peace, speaking consolingly to the depressed, supporting the weak, and demonstrating love consistently in words and actions — letting the love that identifies God's people stay warm in a cooling world.

daily.scripture: Clothe yourselves with humility toward one another, because God opposes the haughty ones, but he gives undeserved kindness to the humble ones.
daily.comment: On the night before he was put to death, Jesus taught Peter and the other apostles an important lesson in humility. Much to the astonishment of his apostles, he did something that a servant would normally do. Jesus took off his outer garments, wrapped a towel around his waist, put water into the basin, and started washing their feet. ( John 13:4, 5 ) It may have taken some time to wash the feet of all 12 apostles​—including Judas, who was going to betray him. Yet, Jesus humbly completed the task. Then Jesus patiently explained: “Do you understand what I have done to you? You address me as ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord,’ and you are correct, for I am such. Therefore, if I, the Lord and Teacher, washed your feet, you also should wash the feet of one another.”​— John 13:12-14 . w25.03 10 ¶9-11 December 14-20

daily.scripture: You guide me with your advice, and afterward you will lead me to glory.
daily.comment: The world makes it challenging for us to remain close to Jehovah. Many reject the idea that God exists. Often, those who ignore what God requires seem to prosper. When we see that happen, our faith can be tested. While we would not deny that God exists, we could begin to wonder whether he will act in our behalf. The writer of Psalm 73 found himself wondering about this. He saw those around him ignoring God’s laws and still enjoying life. As a result, he began to question whether it was worth serving God. ( Ps. 73:11-13 ) What eventually helped the psalmist to correct his view? He meditated on what would happen to those who forget Jehovah. ( Ps. 73:18, 19, 27 ) He also considered the benefits that come from serving God. We too can reflect on the blessings that Jehovah has given us. w24.06 25 ¶16-17 December 14-20

daily.scripture: Let your way of life be free of the love of money.
daily.comment: In Bible times, some took advantage of their poor brothers by charging them interest on the money lent to them. Also, some judges accepted bribes and then judged innocent victims unfairly. Such practices are detestable to Jehovah. ( Ezek. 22:12 ) It is good for us to evaluate our personal attitude toward money. Ask yourself: ‘Do I often find myself thinking about money and what it can buy? If I borrow money, am I slow to repay it, concluding that the person who lent it to me does not need it? Does having money make me feel important but make it hard to be generous? Do I judge my brothers and sisters as materialistic simply because they have money? Do I cultivate friendship with the rich and show little interest in the poor?’ We can protect our friendship with God by keeping our life free of the love of money. If we do so, Jehovah will never leave us! w24.06 12-13 ¶17-18 December 14-20

daily.scripture: I refuse to walk on any evil path, so that I may keep your word.
daily.comment: To guard ourselves against temptation, we need to cultivate right desires. If we learn to “hate what is bad and love what is good,” we will strengthen our resolve to do what is right. ( Amos 5:15 ) Proper desires will also fortify us to remain firm if we find ourselves in a tempting situation. We should be absorbed as much as possible in spiritual activities. When we are at Christian meetings or in the ministry, we build our desire to please Jehovah. ( Matt. 28:19, 20; Heb. 10:24, 25 ) By reading and studying God’s Word and meditating on it, we strengthen our love for what is good and our hatred for what is bad. ( Josh. 1:8; Ps. 1:2, 3; 119:97 ) Remember, Jesus told his disciples: “Pray continually, so that you may not enter into temptation.” ( Matt. 26:41 ) Thus, we take advantage of Jehovah’s help and strengthen our determination to please him.​— Jas. 4:8 . w24.07 17-18 ¶14-16 December 14-20

daily.scripture: I will give you insight and instruct you in the way you should go. I will give you advice with my eye upon you.
daily.comment: Those who provide training do well to imitate the manner in which Jehovah shares his wisdom. Recall that Jehovah gives wisdom generously. Likewise, we freely share our knowledge and experience with those who are learning. We do not withhold some of our knowledge out of fear that the learner may eventually replace us. Nor do we take the view: ‘No one trained me! Let him learn on his own.’ Such an attitude has no place among Jehovah’s people. Rather, we gladly impart not only our knowledge “but also our very selves” to those we train. ( 1 Thess. 2:8 ) We hope that they, “in turn, will be adequately qualified to teach others.” ( 2 Tim. 2:1, 2 ) In that sense, we can be part of an ongoing cycle of generosity that results in a cycle of happiness. w24.09 29 ¶12-13 December 14-20

daily.scripture: Individually we are members belonging to one another.
daily.comment: If you feel that you do not have any outstanding ability, do not be discouraged. No doubt you have qualities that can make you useful in the congregation. You might benefit from prayerfully reading Paul’s reasoning found at 1 Corinthians 12:12-30 . Paul’s words make it clear that you, like every other servant of Jehovah, have a necessary and valuable role to play in the congregation. Do whatever you can to be useful to Jehovah and to your brothers. Be assured that the elders will take your abilities into consideration with regard to any assignments they may give you. ( Rom. 12:4-8 ) All Christians should draw close to Jehovah, experience the joy of giving, and set a good example in Christian living. w24.11 17 ¶12-13 December 14-20

daily.scripture: She began to pray to Jehovah and to weep uncontrollably.
daily.comment: Hannah faced several problems that caused her to shed tears of sorrow. One of these difficulties was that she was in a bigamous marriage, and her husband’s other wife, Peninnah, despised her. As if that were not bad enough, Hannah was childless, while Peninnah had several children. ( 1 Sam. 1:1, 2 ) Peninnah relentlessly taunted Hannah about her barrenness. Hannah was so upset that “she would weep and not eat,” and she became “extremely bitter” at heart. ( 1 Sam. 1:6, 7, 10 ) How did Hannah find comfort? One thing that helped her was that she went to the center of true worship, the tabernacle. There, she begged Jehovah: “Look upon the affliction of your servant and remember me.” ( 1 Sam. 1:11 ) Jehovah saw her distress, heard her cry, and later blessed her by allowing her to conceive.​— 1 Sam. 1:19, 20; 2:21 . w24.12 21 ¶5-7 December 14-20
